Description

ERK1 and ERK2 move into the nucleus within minutes of stimulation, while their activator MEK stays in the cytoplasm. In resting cells MEK holds ERK in the cytoplasm, and ERK leaves MEK when the pathway is activated [1, 2]. ERK2 crosses the nuclear pore without a transport receptor or energy, by binding nucleoporins such as the FG repeats of NUP214 directly [3, 4]. It does so whatever its phosphorylation state: inactive ERK enters too, and in resting cells ERK moves in and out of the nucleus quickly [2, 4, 5]. What concentrates active ERK in the nucleus is therefore its release from MEK in the cytoplasm and its binding to partners in the nucleus. Dimerisation of phosphorylated ERK was proposed to drive its nuclear entry [6], but ERK mutants that cannot dimerise enter the nucleus as fast in living cells, and no dimers were detected there [2, 7].
